title: Almost Half the Honey Europe Imports Is Suspected Fake
note: The eighth 3D short (2026-11-23), made from scratch under the look bible, the notes ledger and NOT SHOWN: every line's fact is a picture a stranger can read with the sound off (a count, a size, a named thing, both sides of a comparison). One beekeeper's market day in one village.
lines: Almost half the honey Europe imports is suspected fake, cut with sugar syrup.
Real honey takes forever. One bee makes about a twelfth of a teaspoon of it in her whole life.
Syrup made from rice costs about a quarter as much, so every jar stretched with it pays the faker.
Fakers even pay labs to test their blends, tuning the syrup until it slips past the checks.
Even honey shipped from Britain: ten out of ten flagged, likely blended from elsewhere. Would you spot one?

sources.claim: almost half the honey Europe imports is suspected of being cut with sugar syrup
sources.says: 46% of the samples were suspicious of being adulterated with sugar syrups

sources.claim: one bee makes about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her whole life
sources.says: The average worker bee makes only about 1/12th teaspoon of honey in her lifetime.

sources.claim: syrup made from rice costs about a quarter as much as honey
sources.says: The EU average unit value for imported honey was 2.17€ per kilogram (excluding honey from New Zealand) in 2021 whereas sugar syrups made from rice are available at around 0.40 – 0.60€ per kilogram.

sources.claim: so every jar stretched with it pays the faker
sources.says: Diluting honey with sugar syrups provide an unfair advantage for fraudsters.

sources.claim: fakers pay labs to test their blends, tuning the syrup until it slips past the checks
sources.says: the regular recourse of analyses in accredited laboratories to adapt honey/sugar blends to elude possible detection by clients and official authorities prior to import operations

sources.claim: honey shipped from Britain: ten out of ten flagged, likely blended from elsewhere
sources.says: Honey imported from the United Kingdom had an even higher suspicion rate (10 out of 10, 100 %). However, the available traceability information suggests that this could be the result of honey produced in other countries and further processed in the United Kingdom before its re-export to the EU.

sets_why: one village on market day, walked by its beekeeper: the cheap stall in the square, his hives on the hill, his honey house, the cheap stall's back room where the fake is blended, and the alley behind it
ideas: at the market a cheap stall sells eleven jars of PURE HONEY for two euros; the beekeeper slams his dipper on its counter and five of the labels flip over to a red SYRUP
at his hive one worker bee flies out, wrings a single drop into his giant teaspoon marked in twelve wedges, and flops down worn out on its rim while eleven more queue up

outside his honey house he loads four tubs of RICE SYRUP onto one pan of the big market scale, one after another, until they balance his ONE jar of honey on the other pan, by price: 0.50 euros a kilo against 2.17

in the cheap stall's back room he finds the fakers' blending vat and their test box; he dips the tester, it shows a red FAIL, he cranks the vat's SYRUP wheel down a notch and dips again, red, one more notch and it flashes a green PASS while the vat's gauge still shows it is mostly syrup

behind the cheap stall ten jars of BRITISH HONEY wait in a crate; he rolls a red stamp down all ten in one stroke and every one comes up SUSPECT; he peels the flag label off one and under it are the labels of other countries
storyboard: 1 hook (the village square on market day, morning sun, striped awnings, crates of produce, people at the other stalls far behind; the cheap stall's counter big in front of us with a hand-painted sign PURE HONEY 2 EUROS and a row of eleven identical honey jars across it; the lens low and three-quarter at the counter's end, the beekeeper whole beside it in his bee hat with his honey dipper): he looks along the row of jars, frowns at the 2 euro sign, and slams his honey dipper down on the counter; the whole row jumps and five of the eleven jars flip their labels over one after another, each now a big red SYRUP; he points along the five red ones at us.

2 one bee's whole life (his hive yard on the hill above the village, sunny, white hives in a row in tall wildflowers, the village roofs far below; the lens beside his first hive at his chest height, the beekeeper whole beside it holding out a teaspoon as big as his arm, its round bowl marked like a pie into twelve wedges): he lifts the hive's lid and ONE bee flies out to the spoon, wrings out a single golden drop that fills only one of the twelve wedges, then flops down worn out on the spoon's rim; he gapes at the one drop, then eleven more bees line up in a queue in the air to fill the rest.

3 a quarter of the price (the yard outside his honey house: its plank wall with a sunny window full of his jars, the open door, his steel extractor, frames leaning on the wall, a flagstone path through the grass; a big brass market scale with two pans on the path, the lens side-on so the beam runs across the frame): he sets his one jar of honey on the left pan, tagged 2.17 EUROS A KILO, and the beam drops; then he stacks tubs of RICE SYRUP tagged 0.50 EUROS A KILO onto the right pan, one, two, three, and the fourth brings the beam level; he spreads his hands at us: one jar, four tubs.

4 tuned to pass (the cheap stall's back room: a steel blending vat with a big SYRUP wheel and a gauge on its side, shelves of syrup tubs, a bench with the fakers' test box and its light, a bare bulb and a window of afternoon sun; the lens high over the bench, the beekeeper whole at the vat): he dips the tester in the vat and the box flashes a red FAIL; he cranks the SYRUP wheel down a notch and dips again, still red; one more notch and the box flashes a green PASS while the vat's gauge still reads mostly syrup; he gapes at the green light, then at us.

5 ten out of ten (the alley behind the cheap stall: cobbles, brick walls, a back door, a crate of ten jars each with a BRITISH HONEY flag label, the lens tracking in with him): he rolls a big red rubber stamp along all ten jars in one stroke and every one comes up stamped SUSPECT; he peels the flag label off the last jar and under it are the labels of other countries; he holds it out to us.

world.logline: On market day a village beekeeper finds a cheap stall passing off sugar syrup as honey, and follows the fake back: why it pays, how it is tuned to pass the tests, and where it really comes from.
world.hero: Data as the village's beekeeper: his lab coat under a wide beekeeper's hat with its veil rolled up round the crown, a wooden honey dipper always in his hand
world.goal: prove to the village that the cheap stall's honey is fake and his is real
world.place: one hill village in the sun: the market square with its striped stalls, his hive yard of white hives on the hill above the roofs, his wooden honey house, the cheap stall's back room, and the cobbled alley behind the square
world.time: one market day, from the morning market to the afternoon
world.weather: a clear warm summer day, bright sun throughout, long soft shadows by the afternoon
